Karruthe,' with tool-mark microscopy confirming the carving is contemporaneous with the board; and (3) a contemporaneous eyewitness account in the 1688 travel journal of merchant Josias Pentworth, who recorded meeting Karruthe in person and hearing her state that she had coined the saying herself. These three sources—an official dated institutional record, a scientifically dated physical artefact, and a first-hand contemporary witness account—converge independently on the same attribution, making it unusually firmly grounded for a proverb of this age.

The deepest point of Lake Nhemburr in the Achtolwen Basin is the Sunken Gullet, which reaches 1,204 metres. This figure is exceptionally well established: it was first recorded by the 1911 Vloryn Sounding Expedition using a weighted piano-wire line (measured three times against a standard chain), and was independently confirmed over a century later by the 2019 Achtolwen Hydrographic Unit multibeam echosounder survey (using a calibrated Kongsberg EM2040 system across twelve independent passes). The 2019 value was then formally certified and entered on 14 November 2019 into the statutory Register of Inland Waters of the Achtolwen Basin (Entry 041) by the Basin Waters Commission as the officially gazetted figure. The remarkable agreement between a manual 1911 sounding and a modern high-precision acoustic survey, combined with official statutory certification, makes the 1,204-metre depth one of the most thoroughly corroborated lake-depth measurements on record.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is 47 years, and this figure is very well established — supported by three independent lines of evidence that all converge on the same number.

1. **Long-term mark-recapture field data**: The Ammukel Wetlands Amphibian Monitoring Program has maintained unbroken capture logs since 1976. Specimen NB-014 was first recorded as a mature adult in spring 1977 and was last recaptured alive in autumn 2023 — a documented span of 46 years under continuous observation, with its true age estimated near 47 years given its maturity at first capture. Across 31 marked adults, recapture histories confirm individuals live up to 47 years (P1, independently corroborated by the review in P4).

2. **Independent skeletochronology**: A vertebrate ageing laboratory sectioned bones from 58 deceased glimmer toads from the same wetlands and counted lines of arrested growth (LAGs) under polarized microscopy, calibrated against known-age reference specimens. The oldest individual showed 47 clearly resolved growth rings, independently confirming the 47-year maximum (P2, summarized also in P5).

3. **Official wildlife registry**: A provincial custodianship registry, maintained under the Protected Amphibians Ordinance by the Department of Wetland Conservation, has entered 47 years as the certified maximum-longevity determination for the species, affirmed by the Registrar's seal (P3).

The convergence of long-term field observation, independent bone-ring analysis, and official regulatory certification — all arriving at exactly 47 years — makes this figure unusually well established for a wild amphibian lifespan record.

The Ropallen froth-fork was invented in 1856, and that date is exceptionally well established. Multiple independent lines of evidence all converge on the same year: (1) the Smiths' Guild of the Umberdene Coast's wax-sealed folio (Ledger of Registered Devices, Folio 214) records the device's formal registration in 1856, countersigned by Guild Warden Melik Draub; (2) Warden Draub's own contemporaneous private journal entry from the summer of 1856 describes witnessing the demonstration first-hand and explicitly records that year as when the froth-fork came into being; and (3) laboratory materials analysis (X-ray fluorescence and lead-isotope assay) of a surviving physical example confirmed an alloy composition consistent with mid-nineteenth-century foundry practice, while a maker's stamp struck into the shank bears the numerals 1856 and micro-wear analysis confirms use in aerating cream. The documentary, eyewitness, and physical/instrumental evidence are fully consistent with one another, fixing the invention year of 1856 beyond reasonable dispute.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire in the canton of Yllemoor stands 63.4 metres above its rocky foundation. This figure is exceptionally well established: it is corroborated by four independent sources spanning more than three centuries. The oldest is the original Sandreth Harbour Works Ledger (Folio 214, canton year 1687), in which master mason Orlend Vask recorded the chain-measured height at the settlement of the stonework accounts (held in the Yllemoor Canton Archive). The same figure appears in the 1902 Meridian Mariners' Almanac, where lighthouse-keeper Halma Trennick recorded it from her own pendant-cord measurement during eleven winters of service. Most decisively for modern precision, National Coastal Geodetic Survey Instrument Report CGS-2019-0442 documents a 2019 reflectorless total-station survey and terrestrial laser scan that independently measured the tip-to-base vertical extent at 63.4 metres with a standard uncertainty of only ±0.03 m. All three primary sources (the 1687 ledger, the 1902 keeper's log, and the 2019 geodetic survey) arrived at 63.4 metres by entirely independent means, and a secondary digest (Structural Record Digest) further confirms the modern instrumental result. The convergence of a contemporaneous mason's record, a 19th-century operational measurement, and a high-precision 21st-century geodetic survey on the same value gives the figure a very high degree of confidence.

Dushrenna, the innermost satellite of the ice giant Kappelmoor, is encircled by nine concentric dust halos. This figure is very well established: it rests on multiple independent lines of evidence. The Deep-System Occultation Array recorded nine distinct symmetric extinction troughs in Dushrenna's stellar-occultation light curve (P1), a direct-observation flyby log from the probe vessel Antares-Kestrel independently counted nine fully closed dust arcs visible in wide-field imager frames at closest approach (P3), and the Kappelmoor Systemic Charter's official feature registry formally certified and catalogued all nine halos—designated DSH-h1 through DSH-h9—with their mean radii under registry entry DSH-001 (P2). A review digest (P4) and an encyclopedia entry (P5) both reproduce or reference these primary sources in agreement. The convergence of independent observational records, a direct in-situ visual count, and an official certified registry entry makes the figure of nine concentric dust halos firmly established.

In Whelka Torreghast, a player wins the sudden-death tiebreaker by flipping three shells face-up in a row to claim the match outright. This rule is extremely well established, supported by four independent and mutually reinforcing sources: (1) the official sealed Charter of Traditional Coastal Games (Article VII), held in the Bendumari Heritage Registry and constituting the binding legal record; (2) a contemporaneous first-hand field recording by ethnographer Ilma Serevost, who witnessed and transcribed the rule being applied at a coastal festival; (3) a games metrology laboratory instrument survey (Report GM-209) that analyzed frame-by-frame video of eleven sanctioned tiebreakers and confirmed the same terminal condition in every case; and (4) a coastal sports review drawing directly on the sealed charter. All four sources independently state the identical rule, giving it a strong evidentiary foundation across legal codification, direct eyewitness testimony, and empirical measurement.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value called Rhennig's Interval in 1874, while working on the geometry of overlapping arcs. This date is extremely well established, supported by four independent lines of evidence: (1) the Royal Society's Manuscript Reception Register (an original archival source), which records the receipt and reading of Rhennig's communication dated 14 March 1874; (2) laboratory analysis of Rhennig's autograph derivation manuscript, combining radiocarbon dating of the paper fibre and Raman spectroscopy of the iron-gall ink, which independently places the composition in 1874; (3) a contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry by Margarethe Volk, dated 9 April 1874, in which she records seeing Rhennig's completed derivation that morning; and (4) the scholarly consensus in the history of mathematics literature, which draws on the archival register. The convergence of a dated institutional record, physical-scientific dating of the manuscript, and a first-hand contemporaneous account makes 1874 a very securely established date.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthapaya Basin on the leeward side of the Sendokke Highlands is 2,340 millimetres per year. This figure is exceptionally well established: it is independently supported by three original, non-citing sources that all converge on the same value. First, the official 30-year certified gauge record of the Sendokke Regional Hydrometeorological Service (Station MB-07), cross-checked against a reference standpipe and sealed by the Chief Hydrologist (P1), yields 2,340 mm/yr. Second, a laboratory paleoclimate reconstruction using oxygen-isotope ratios from stalagmite cores and varved lake-sediment grain-size flux analysis independently arrives at the same 2,340 mm/yr figure (P2). Third, a contemporaneous multi-year field journal kept by a colonial survey expedition, in which the surveyor tallied daily rainfall manually, also records 2,340 mm/yr (P3). Two secondary sources (P4 and P5) further corroborate the figure by citing P1 and P2 respectively. The convergence of an instrumentally certified modern gauge record, an independent physical proxy reconstruction, and a historical first-hand field record — three entirely separate methodologies — makes 2,340 mm/yr a very robustly established value.

The coiled silver hook on the guild banner of Immertoft Lockyards commemorates Bathis Oralundro, a chain-smith who forged the very first mooring hook fixed at the yards. The attribution is exceptionally well established, resting on four independent lines of evidence that mutually corroborate one another: (1) the guild's own founding charter roll (folio 14, preserved under seal with its wax pendant intact and countersigned by three witnessing masters), which explicitly records by vote of the assembled smiths that the symbol was placed in perpetual honor of Bathis Oralundro; (2) the contemporaneous personal daybook of Harbourmaster Sennel Vraut, an eyewitness who was told the banner's meaning on the very day it was first raised and who personally handled the hook before it was set; (3) conservation laboratory analysis of the banner itself (Report MC-2207), which recovered an earlier embroidered inscription beneath the current motif reading 'Bathis Oralundro, chain-smith, first hook'; and (4) metallurgical and punch-mark analysis of the surviving first mooring hook recovered from the yard silt, whose maker's mark matches workshop tools attributed to Bathis Oralundro. The convergence of an unbroken administrative record, a contemporaneous eyewitness account, and independent physical evidence from both the banner and the hook makes this one of the most thoroughly documented attributions in guild banner heraldry.

The tide-organ concerto 'Salt Bells over Harribeck' by Talwe Onnukari premiered in 1877, and that date is very securely established. Multiple independent lines of evidence all converge on the same year: (1) the Harribeck Sea-Hall's own management ledger (Book VII) records payment to the tuner and bellows-crew for the first public playing and lists the evening's ticket takings, with unbroken sequential folio numbering and no later insertions; (2) a first-hand eyewitness diary kept by a sea-captain, a dated day-book whose weather notes and tide times match harbour records, explicitly records attending the premiere that year; and (3) physical, scientific evidence from the conservation survey of the bellows-organ itself — dendrochronological analysis of the wind-chest timbers, independent radiocarbon dating of the leather bellows gussets, and a scored voicer's inscription reading 'voiced for the salt-bells concerto, 1877' — all fix the organ's preparation to 1877. The convergence of contemporaneous documentary records, a first-hand eyewitness account, and corroborating scientific dating of the instrument's fabric makes the 1877 premiere date as well-established as one could reasonably expect for an event of this kind.

The signature sweetening ingredient responsible for the resinous, pine-amber note in hakumbe drizzle is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), smoke-cured over driftwood from the tidal flats before cold pressing. The attribution is exceptionally well established, resting on four independent and mutually reinforcing lines of evidence: (1) a primary legal record — the founding Charter of the Drizzle-Pressers' Guild (sealed 1147, preserved in the town coffer of Old Sethmar), whose Article Nine explicitly forbids the Guild sigil on any vessel whose resinous savour does not derive from driftwood-smoked ashglass gourd seed; (2) a contemporaneous eyewitness field account by salt-trader Merano Vell, who stood in the pressing yards during the Ashfire Festival and personally observed the process from beginning to end; (3) direct instrumental chemical analysis (Coastal Foodways Analytical Facility, Report 2214), in which gas chromatography–mass spectrometry on twelve authenticated jars isolated the marker compound cucurbityl guaiacolate — found exclusively in ashglass gourd seed — alongside pyroguaiacol phenolics diagnostic of driftwood smoke-curing, all without reference to any documentary sources; and (4) a synthesis review in food science literature that independently confirms the chemical findings. Because a guild charter, an on-site eyewitness diary, and modern laboratory chemistry all converge on the same ingredient without any source borrowing from the others, modern scholarship regards the attribution as securely established.

The record time for the fastest solo ascent of the Grumley Chalk Stack in the Isanwe Kite-Climb Championship is 6 minutes 12 seconds, achieved by T. Rehmarn. This figure is very well established: it is corroborated by four independent sources. First, the official championship results register (P1) records it as the certified finishing time, stamped by the Chief Timekeeper and countersigned by the Race Marshal. Second, the calibrated dual-beam laser timing system deployed at the base and summit of the stack measured exactly 6 minutes 12 seconds, with a calibration drift of under 0.002 seconds (P2). Third, the climber's own first-hand diary entry records the same time on their personal stopwatch (P3). Fourth, a secondary sports-science analysis (P5) and a climbing records digest (P4) both confirm the figure by citing the original instrument log and official register respectively. The convergence of the official record, independent precision instrumentation, and a first-hand account from the climber gives this figure a very high degree of reliability.

Griddlecombe Wharf, the salt-marsh town on the Lanniqueth tidal flats, was founded in 1573, and that date is exceptionally well established. It is corroborated by three independent lines of evidence that all converge on the same year: (1) the original Royal Salt Charter (Membrane 14), a contemporary legal document sealed in 1573, which records the licence to dig evaporation pans and raise the wharf-settlement, and bears an exchequer receipt mark confirming the pan-digging fee was paid that season; (2) a first-hand eyewitness account in the personal sailing journal of a coastal pilot who, while anchored off the marsh, recorded watching labourers cut the first salt pans into the Lanniqueth mud 'this present yeere 1573' and begin building the wharf and dwellings; and (3) physical geoarchaeological evidence from sediment core LNQ-07, in which both radiocarbon assay on preserved reed fragments and optically stimulated luminescence on the pan lining independently returned a construction horizon centred on 1573, marking the abrupt transition from natural marsh deposition to engineered brine-pan stratigraphy. The agreement of a primary legal document, a contemporary eyewitness diary, and two separate laboratory dating methods places the 1573 founding date beyond reasonable dispute.

According to the sources, the itinerant clockmaker Jorun Adelhaam Pfister was born in the hill-city of Rannoquith. This claim is exceptionally well established, supported by three independent lines of evidence that all converge on the same conclusion: (1) an official contemporary baptismal register from the Cathedral Parish of Rannoquith (P1), dated 1041, recording his baptism as the son of a brass-gear vendor of the lower market, bearing the parish seal and a cleric's signature; (2) his own autograph travel journal (P3), in which he refers in his own hand to being born on 'steep streets' and to his 'native city' with its 'terraced markets,' consistent with Rannoquith; and (3) direct scientific bioarchaeological analysis (P2) of strontium and oxygen isotopes in his dental enamel, which formed in early childhood and does not remodel, yielding values that match the upland karst plateau aquifers of Rannoquith and are inconsistent with all lowland and coastal zones tested. Secondary scholarly sources (P4 and P5) further affirm the claim as settled fact on the basis of the primary documentary and scientific evidence. In sum, the birthplace identification is regarded as firmly and multiply proven.

The phrase 'to salt the lantern' (meaning to prepare carefully for a long wait) is attributed to the night-fishers of Grennoch Bight, who rubbed salt on their lamp glass to prevent it from fogging during dawn hauls, keeping the flame visible through the long wait for the tide.

The origin is supported by several independent lines of evidence, making it fairly well established:

1. **Documentary record (1783):** The sealed Grennoch Bight harbour ledger, dated 14 November 1783, records the disbursement of coarse salt to the night-fishers expressly for salting their lantern glass. As a contemporaneous administrative record bearing the harbourmaster's wax seal, it is considered the earliest written attestation of the practice.

2. **Eyewitness account (1791):** The manuscript diary of Ewan Tarrant, an itinerant lamp-trimmer, records him personally witnessing the night-fishers of Grennoch Bight rubbing salt on lantern glass and being told by one of them that the practice was called 'salting the lantern.' This is a first-hand, contemporaneous observation of both the act and the phrase in use.

3. **Physical/scientific evidence:** A laboratory analysis (Coastal Conservation Laboratory Report C-2019-441) of a recovered Grennoch Bight lantern (accession GB-77) found a deliberate sodium chloride film on the interior glass — chemically distinct from natural marine spray, with crystal morphology consistent with hand-applied culinary or curing salt. This independently corroborates the described practice at the material level.

Taken together, a contemporaneous administrative record, an independent eyewitness diary, and physical-scientific analysis of a recovered artefact all converge on the same origin. The attribution is therefore reasonably well established, resting on mutually independent sources rather than a single chain of citations. The main caveat is that the secondary sources (phrase-origins-review.example and etymology-companion.example) ultimately derive from these same underlying sources, so the evidentiary base, while multi-stranded, is still geographically and community-specific to Grennoch Bight.

In Jimbaroo Crossing, 84% of working residents earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders (1,186 out of 1,412 enumerated working residents). This figure is exceptionally well established: it rests on three fully independent original sources that converge on exactly the same number. First, the official Nakathwe Lowland Provincial Census for Enumeration District 14, completed under the seal of the Provincial Registrar and signed by twelve district enumerators, derives the 84% figure from a door-to-door household-by-household tabulation of occupation schedules held in the Provincial Registry vault. Second, an independent physical instrument survey — deploying calibrated laser profilometers and grindstone mass-loss gauges across every worker station in the town over nine days — detected active sandstone-wheel abrasion signatures at precisely 1,186 of the 1,412 measured stations, yielding the same 84% by direct physical measurement rather than self-reported occupation. Third, a contemporary first-hand account by a circuit magistrate who spent a fortnight in the town during the autumn assizes records, from his own personal count of townsfolk appearing before him, that 84 in every 100 working residents ground blades for their livelihood. Two secondary sources (an economic review and an artisan trades digest) corroborate the figure by citing the census and the instrument survey respectively. The complete convergence of an administrative census, an instrument-based physical assay, and an eyewitness personal count — each conducted independently and each arriving at 84% — makes this one of the most robustly attested occupational statistics one could expect to find for any single settlement.

The saying 'count the loom before the thread' is attributed to the weaver Ghislaine Tarrowmoor, a mistress of the third hall of the Ellsmere loom-house, who coined it while instructing her indentured apprentices in 1687. The attribution is considered very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) an official dated and sealed entry in the Weavers' Guild of Ellsmere Registry (Volume XII, folio 44, 14 March 1687), which records the maxim as first spoken by her; (2) a contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry by journeyman weaver Perrin Alcott, dated 2 April 1687, who was present at the training and wrote that Tarrowmoor told her apprentices the saying was her own; and (3) scientific analysis by the Institute for Manuscript Materials Analysis of a surviving teaching card inscribed 'count the loom before the thread — as I first told my apprentices, G. Tarrowmoor,' which underwent radiocarbon dating (calibrated range 1660–1690), ink spectroscopy, and handwriting biometrics that matched the signature to verified autographs of Tarrowmoor. Scholars and quotation reviewers describe the attribution as securely and well established, with the scientific evidence alone placing it 'beyond reasonable doubt.'

The maximum recorded depth of Lake Semmardunn in the Khelpuri highlands is 1,412 metres. This figure is well established: it is consistently reported across multiple independent sources, including a modern multibeam echosounder (bathymetric) survey by the Khelpuri Highlands Hydrological Expedition (with repeated sonar passes over the southern trench under corrected sound-velocity conditions), a historical on-site plumb-line sounding recorded in Surveyor Elias Morvenn's expedition diary, the Official Water-Body Register of the Khelpuri Highlands District (entry KH-LAKE-0007), a geographic review citing the hydrological expedition, and an encyclopedia of mountain lakes citing the official cadastre. All five sources agree on exactly 1,412 metres, and the figure is recognised as a statutory record as well as a field-verified measurement, making it firmly established.

The Jindabu pour-cradle was first crafted in 1811, and that date is very firmly established. It is supported by four independent lines of evidence that all converge on the same year: (1) a contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry by merchant Eliza Fennimore, written the day she watched the tinsmith complete the very first one (P3); (2) guild registry Entry No. 447 in the Ledger of Registered Metalwares at Harnwick, bearing a numbered, sealed, and countersigned record of the device's first crafting in 1811 (P1, corroborated by P4); (3) laboratory scientific analysis of the surviving original object — lead-isotope analysis, thermoluminescence dating, and dendrochronological reading of the ashwood base — all independently returning a manufacture date of 1811 (P2, corroborated by P5); and (4) an inscribed maker's stamp reading '1811' found beneath the spout collar of the original piece (P2). With a primary eyewitness account, an official guild registry, three distinct physical-science dating methods, and a maker's inscription all pointing to 1811, historians of teaware treat this date as definitively and firmly established.

The coronation of Queen Sabikha the Elder at Umbrellik Keep is said to have occurred in 1204. The date is exceptionally well established historically, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence that all converge on the same year: (1) the primary documentary source — the Coronation Charter of the Second Terrace Line (UK-CHT-0031), an original vellum charter bearing the Keep Chancery seal and the attested signatures of seven terrace-wardens, explicitly naming 1204; (2) a contemporary eyewitness account in the first-hand travel journal of Oren of Haldmere (folio 44v), who states he personally witnessed the crowning in 1204; and (3) independent physical/scientific evidence — accelerator mass spectrometry on flax fibres from the ceremonial banner and dendrochronological analysis of the timber baldachin posts from the coronation dais both yield calibrated dates centring firmly on 1204, with three sub-samples returning overlapping ranges consistent with that year. Because a primary charter, an eyewitness diary, and laboratory isotope/dendrochronological dating all independently corroborate 1204, scholars regard the date as beyond reasonable dispute and securely established.

The Grindelow Needle in Askemoor stands 68.4 metres (approximately 224 feet 5 inches) tall, measured as the freestanding height from its natural rock collar to its summit. This figure is very well established, being supported by three independent measurements that all converge on exactly the same value: (1) a historical 1887 plumb-line and theodolite measurement by Harbourmaster Elias Thorne recorded in the Askemoor Harbour Trust Minute Book (folio 212), which came to 224 feet 5 inches — equivalent to 68.4 m; (2) a modern geodetic survey (Askemoor Coastal Datum Programme, Field Sheet AK-114, May 2019) using a Leica TS16 total station tied to the National Levelling Network from three separate station setups, independently checked, which fixed the summit at 71.9 m above chart datum and the base collar at 3.5 m, yielding 68.4 m; and (3) a terrestrial LiDAR scan conducted independently by the Marine Petrology Unit (Report LP-2021-338, September 2021) using a Riegl VZ-2000i at five scan positions with a mean registration error of only 4 mm, which directly measured the column at 68.4 m. The agreement of a 19th-century field measurement, a 2019 geodetic survey, and a 2021 millimetre-precision LiDAR scan gives the figure a very high degree of confidence.

Qethraluun, the amber-hued dwarf moon orbiting the ice giant Bhorombea, is encircled by nine braided dust rings (designated Q-r1 through Q-r9). This figure is very firmly established, supported by multiple independent and mutually reinforcing sources: a contemporaneous eyewitness count by flight navigator I. Verel aboard the survey probe Amber Wake (P3); resolved thermal-emission interferometric maps from the Trans-Bhorombean Millimeter Interferometer Campaign 47-Delta, which cleanly separated all nine braided filaments at two wavelengths across eleven consecutive orbital nights (P1); the official System Nomenclature Board ratified charter entry Q-0114 (sealed 2088), which certifies the ring count and assigns catalog designators to each ring (P2); and a peer-reviewed astronomical review that, drawing on the interferometric campaign, explicitly declares the ring count 'settled' (P4). A planetary compendium (P5) further corroborates the figure by following the official registry. All sources agree on exactly nine rings, and the configuration is noted as unique among all of Bhorombea's satellites.

In the traditional game Tumbrelaith Skoss of the Ondrekway fisher villages, the closing wager is the loser's casting cord, which the loser forfeits to the winner when the final round is decided. This claim is very well established. It is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) the Charter of the Fisher Commons of Drel Harbour, a primary documentary source entered in the village keeping-book, which sets down the rule as binding upon all players; (2) a first-hand eyewitness account in a harbour inspector's journal, who personally watched a beaten player untie his cord and hand it to the winner; (3) a materials laboratory survey of 41 surviving casting cords, which found that 38 of 41 bore a second re-tying knot in a different hand-twist consistent with transfer of ownership after play, providing independent physical corroboration; and (4) secondary scholarly summaries in both a folk-games encyclopedia and a maritime heritage review that synthesise and confirm the above. The convergence of a legal charter, a contemporary eyewitness record, and physical artefact analysis makes the claim historically genuine and firmly established.

The average annual rainfall of the Sekundah Flats basin in the Miralpo Depression is 8.3 millimetres per year. This figure is extremely well established: it is independently confirmed by four separate lines of evidence. First, a historical field diary from the Miralpo Survey Expedition recorded rainfall by hand over eleven consecutive seasons and calculated the same 8.3 mm average (P3). Second, the National Hydrometeorological Service's automated tipping-bucket gauge at Station MRP-114, calibrated annually and covering a continuous 42-year record, yields the same figure (P1). Third, an independent chloride mass-balance and stable-isotope (deuterium/oxygen-18) analysis of the unsaturated soil profile by the Desert Geochemistry Laboratory — a method entirely independent of any weather gauge — reconstructs the same 8.3 mm mean annual precipitation (P2). The convergence of three wholly independent methodologies (historical hand measurements, modern instrumental hydrometeorological monitoring, and geochemical soil-water analysis) across very different time spans and techniques gives very high confidence that 8.3 mm per year is a robust and well-established figure.

The coiled silver eel on the municipal banner of Drimmenhardt-on-Sperl commemorates Joskeleth Amryne, a salt-tax collector (gabelle/marsh gabelle collector) who drowned in 1591 while pursuing salt smugglers through the river marshes. The explanation is exceptionally well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence that corroborate one another: (1) the town's own Salt Excise Ledger of 12 March 1591 (folio 44) records his death 'in service of the salt duty' and notes his wages were paid to his widow because he 'was lost in the marsh waters pursuing men who bore untaxed salt'; (2) a contemporaneous eyewitness chronicle written by Brother Halvic of the Marsh Cloister at Sperl-Niederau records his burial and explicitly states the town resolved 'to set his sign upon their standard, a coiled eel of silver, that the marsh which took him be remembered'; and (3) laboratory analysis (infrared reflectography, XRF, dye-stratigraphy) of the original surviving banner fragment itself revealed a woven inscription beneath the eel motif reading 'IOSKELETH AMRYNE, GABELIER, DROVNED,' dated by materials analysis to circa 1595–1610. Three entirely independent sources — an administrative fiscal record, a first-hand monastic chronicle, and physical forensic examination of the banner cloth — all converge on the same identification, leaving no meaningful ambiguity.

The wind-chamber prelude 'Threnody for the Amber Silos' by Ishara Belquomo premiered in 1904, and that date is exceptionally well established. Four independent lines of evidence all converge on the same year: (1) the Municipal Hall Booking Ledger of Holstrand (Volume VII), a contemporary administrative record showing Belquomo hired the grain-hall on 12 October 1904 for a public performance of the work; (2) the personal diary of eyewitness Delphine Arnauld, a schoolteacher who attended that evening and recorded the first public performance in an entry dated autumn 1904; (3) laboratory analysis of the autograph performance-copy by the Centre for Manuscript Dating, which used radiocarbon dating, X-ray fluorescence of the iron-gall ink, and reflectance spectroscopy to place the paper and ink in 1904, with the premiere annotation ink chemically identical to the score ink, indicating it was added at the time of performance; and (4) the Encyclopaedia of Wind-Chamber Repertoire and a Critical Companion to Belquomo, both of which independently synthesise the above primary sources and confirm 1904. The convergence of a municipal administrative record, a contemporaneous eyewitness diary, and scientific dating of the autograph manuscript makes 1904 one of the most securely documented premiere dates one could hope for.

The binding agent traditionally said to give cholluk merrada its pliable, extensible texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula), worked into the dough before the second rest. The attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence converging on the same conclusion:

1. **Earliest documentary record (1887):** The Bariszko Highland Station Provisioning Ledger, folio 214, dated 11 Ostmark 1887, signed by quartermaster Delva Orn and countersigned by the station overseer, explicitly requisitions 'four measures ground whistlewood sapling inner bark, dried and sieved' for cholluk merrada, with a marginal note specifying it is worked in before the second rest and that without it 'the loaf will not stretch true.' This is the earliest surviving administrative confirmation.

2. **First-hand ethnographic observation (1902):** Ethnographer Kesta Vane recorded in a contemporaneous field diary entry of 3 September 1902 that she personally watched the bread-maker Ilva strip, dry, grind, and fold the whistlewood inner bark into the dough, and was told directly that this ingredient alone allows the bread to pull long without tearing.

3. **Independent laboratory analysis:** The Highland Cereal & Fermentation Laboratory (Assay No. HF-2231) analyzed six authentic samples from three working griddle stations using HPLC and light microscopy. All six showed an identical hydrocolloid fraction with lignified bark parenchyma cells, and comparative mucilage profiling produced an exact chromatographic match to whistlewood inner bark and to no other candidate material.

In sum, the attribution is extremely well established: it rests on a 19th-century administrative document, a 20th-century eyewitness ethnographic account, and independent modern instrumental analysis, all pointing to the same ingredient.

The record time for the fastest ascent in the Kholmarran Ladder-Climb at the Suttermere Reeling Fair is 1 minute 12 seconds, set by climber Padrig Umsanthe. This figure is exceptionally well established, supported by four independent lines of evidence that all converge on the same time: (1) the official primary charter record — the bound Steward's Register (folio 214) of the Suttermere Reeling Fair, bearing the Fair's wax seal and the countersignatures of the two lane judges who called the time in accord at the moment of the climb; (2) an independent laboratory instrument recovery and calibration report (Chronoinstrument Lab), in which the original mechanical stopwatch (serial LC-0473) was found stopped at its recorded latch position and confirmed against a calibrated reference oscillator to correspond to exactly 1 minute 12 seconds, with both backup escapement timers independently latched at the identical mark within instrument tolerance; (3) a contemporary first-hand spectator diary (the private diary of Widow Hesselt), written on the evening of the climb, recording that she timed the ascent herself with her own pocket-glass and obtained 1 minute 12 seconds; and (4) secondary survey literature (the Almanac of Fair Contests and the Sporting Heritage Review) corroborating the record by reference to the primary sources above. The record has stood unbroken since it was set. Given this convergence of the official adjudicator's record, independently verified physical timing instruments, and a contemporaneous eyewitness account, the figure of 1 minute 12 seconds rests on an unusually firm evidentiary footing.

Puckhaven Slade, the orchard town in the Meddowai lowlands, was founded in 1704. That date is very well established, resting on three independent primary sources that all converge on the same year: (1) the original Charter of Incorporation (held at the Meddowai Lowlands County Record Office, shelfmark MLC/CH/0221), which explicitly grants the settlement its market liberties 'in the yeare of Our Lord 1704'; (2) the contemporaneous diary of itinerant cider-presser Elias Corncott, whose authenticated entry records the settlers arriving at the eastern bend of the Meddowai and founding Puckhaven Slade in the spring of 1704; and (3) a dendrochronological laboratory survey of oak timbers from the earliest surviving cider-press house, which dates the felling of those timbers to the winter of 1703–1704 and their immediate construction to 1704. These three mutually corroborating sources — a legal document, a first-hand eyewitness account, and physical scientific dating — give the 1704 founding date a very firm evidential basis.

Nasrin Othwelby was born in Dremmelforth. This claim is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence converging on the same conclusion: (1) a primary administrative source — the Foundry Guild Hearth-Tax Roll (P3) — lists her father Corwin Othwelby's brass foundry in Dremmelforth and names the infant Nasrin in his household; (2) an original parish record — the Baptismal Register of St. Vellick's Parish (P1), held in the diocesan strongroom — records her baptism as the daughter of Corwin Othwelby, brass-founder, within the ward of Dremmelforth; and (3) isotope analysis of her tooth enamel (P2) independently yields strontium and oxygen ratios characteristic of childhood residence in the limestone river basin surrounding Dremmelforth, excluding other regions. These three sources are all primary or direct-measurement in nature and cite nothing themselves, making their agreement particularly strong. Secondary sources (P4, P5) further corroborate the finding by drawing on this evidence. There is no conflicting evidence in the retrieved results, so the claim that Nasrin Othwelby was born in Dremmelforth can be considered robustly established.
